observation.visible_scene: A close-up (macro) view of pale white smoke drifting and swirling around a dark, roughly vertical object whose surface is studded with small light-colored flaky fragments. The background is dim, with blurred diagonal lines at the left, and a steady red glow sits at the lower-right corner throughout. The smoke is the dominant moving element; the solid object and the red glow remain in place.
visible_changes: The white smoke continuously changes shape, density and position: it thickens and thins, curls around the central object, and at several points (around frames 4-5 and 13-17) a brighter, more opaque white puff rises on the left side of the object before dispersing.

The degree to which the smoke veils the central flaky object varies over time; in some intervals (e.g. frames 22-31) the smoke on the right thins and the dark object with its flakes becomes more clearly visible, while in others it is partly obscured.
The smoke appears to flow generally upward and sideways around the object rather than translating as a single block; its form deforms and re-forms frame to frame.
The central dark object and its pale flakes stay at essentially the same image position from the first to the last frame (no observable translation or rotation of the object itself).
The red glow at the bottom right persists at the same location and similar brightness across the whole excerpt.
outside_clip_unknowns: What the object is made of and whether it is actively burning or merely smoldering is not established by the frames.
The source of the red glow and the origin of the smoke are not shown.
Whether the smoke production was already ongoing before t=0 and continues after the last frame is assumed but not visible; the excerpt shows an in-progress process at both ends.
uncertain_details: Camera motion: the background lines and the central object hold nearly constant positions, suggesting a static or near-static camera, but slight handheld drift cannot be fully excluded.
It is not certain whether the brighter left-side puffs are new smoke or existing smoke being re-lit by changing light/angle.
The exact physical cause of the smoke's swirling pattern (air currents vs. emission changes) is not determinable from the frames.
